slide.title: Your First Support Automation
slide.body: Three connected blocks: form icon → AI spark icon → sheet icon, drawn like a row of dominoes. Small tag: AI for Customer Experience and Support · Lesson 8.

scenes.voiceover: On many support teams, someone reads every contact form message each morning, decides which team should handle it, and copies it into a spreadsheet. Today you build a small automation that does this for you, with no code at all.

slide.title: Automating Simple Tasks with n8n or Zapier
slide.body: AI for Customer Experience and Support · Lesson 8 of 12 · Screen demo

scenes.voiceover: In the last lesson, we designed the hand-off. Today we automate a simple, low-risk task. An automation tool connects apps and runs steps for you when something happens. Two popular tools are Zapier and n8n, and we use them in the browser, with no installation.

slide.title: Trigger → AI step → Action
slide.body: Three boxes with arrows: Trigger ('new form response') → AI step ('add one label from a fixed list') → Action ('add a row to a sheet').

scenes.voiceover: A simple AI automation has three parts. The trigger is the event that starts it, such as a new form response. The AI step reads the message and does something with it, such as adding one label from a fixed list. And the action does something with the result, such as adding a row to a spreadsheet.

slide.title: What we automate
slide.body: Automate (green): label + log each message. Not here (grey): automatic replies to customers. A person still reads every message.

scenes.voiceover: This is the triage idea from lesson five, running on its own. Following your workflow map, labelling is a good step to automate. A wrong label in a log is low risk, and a person still reads each message. We do not send automatic replies to customers here.

scenes.on_screen_text: Check the plan. Use made-up data.
scenes.voiceover: Some practical points. Free plan limits change often, so check the current plan before you start. Some AI steps may need a separate account. And test with made-up data only. Never connect a real customer inbox to a trial account.

scenes.stock_query: row of dominoes falling close up
scenes.on_screen_text: Test the chain before you rely on it
scenes.voiceover: Think of a row of dominoes. When the first one falls, the trigger, it knocks the next one, the AI step, which knocks the last one, the action. If one domino is in the wrong place, the chain stops. So test the row before you rely on it.

scenes.stock_query: outdoor equipment shop tents and backpacks
scenes.voiceover: Let's build it. Aroha runs support for a hypothetical outdoor equipment shop in Wellington, New Zealand. She wants each contact form message labelled order, product question, return or other, and logged in a sheet.

screen_steps: Open Google Forms and create a form titled 'Contact us (test)'
Add three fields: Name, Email, Message
Submit two made-up test responses
Open Google Sheets and create a sheet called 'Support log'
Type column headers in row 1: Date, Email, Message, Label
scenes.voiceover: First, the test data. I create a form called contact us test, with name, email and message. I submit two made-up responses. Then I create a sheet called support log, with four columns: date, email, message and label.

screen_steps: Log in to Zapier and click 'Create', then 'Zap' (or the current button for a new automation)
Choose trigger app 'Google Forms' and event 'New Form Response'
Connect the test Google account and select the 'Contact us (test)' form
Click 'Test trigger' and show the sample response loading
scenes.voiceover: Now I log in to Zapier and create a new automation. For the trigger, I choose Google Forms, and the event new form response. I connect my test account, choose the form, and test the trigger. A sample response loads.

screen_steps: Add a second step and choose the built-in AI option (for example 'AI by Zapier')
Type the instruction: 'Read the message. Reply with exactly one label from this list: Order, Product question, Return, Other. If unsure, reply Other.'
Map the Message field from step 1 into the input
Click 'Test step' and zoom in on the output: a single label
scenes.voiceover: Next, the AI step. I add the built-in AI option and write the instruction. Read the message. Reply with exactly one label from this list: order, product question, return, other. If unsure, reply other. I map the message field into the input, and test. The output is one label only.

screen_steps: Add a third step: app 'Google Sheets', event 'Create Spreadsheet Row'
Select the 'Support log' sheet
Map Date, Email, Message and the AI label to the four columns
Click 'Test step', then switch to the sheet and highlight the new row
scenes.on_screen_text: Step 3: Log it in the sheet
scenes.voiceover: Then the action. I choose Google Sheets and the event create spreadsheet row. I pick the support log sheet and map the date, email, message and AI label to the columns. I test the step, open the sheet, and there is the new row.

screen_steps: Turn the automation on (publish it)
Submit a new made-up form response
Refresh the 'Support log' sheet and show the new labelled row
Optional: show a still of the same three-node flow on the n8n canvas (only if node names are confirmed)
scenes.voiceover: Finally, I turn the automation on, submit a new test message, and check the sheet again. In n8n cloud, the same flow uses a form trigger, an AI node and a Google Sheets node.

slide.title: Improving the instruction
slide.body:
Message: 'Is the blue tent waterproof and can I return it if not?' → fits two labels.
Added to instruction: 'Label mixed messages by the first question.'

scenes.voiceover: Aroha tests ten made-up messages. One asks, is the blue tent waterproof, and can I return it if not? It fits two labels. So she updates her instruction: label mixed messages by the first question.
A common mistake is to turn an automation on after one good test, and never look again. A field is renamed, a connection expires, or a run limit is reached, and it stops without warning.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Trigger → AI step → action. 2. Automate low-risk steps; people own replies. 3. Check limits, use made-up data, check run history.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a simple AI automation has three parts: a trigger, an AI step and an action. Second, start with low-risk steps like labelling and logging, and keep people responsible for replies. Third, plans and interfaces change often, so check the limits, test with made-up data, and check the run history, because automations can fail silently.

Now build your own. In the exercise, you will create the same three-step automation in Zapier or n8n, submit ten made-up messages, count the correct labels, and improve your instruction once. Next week, you build your capstone, starting with the next lesson: build your support assistant. See you there.
